preamble: Insertion of the alveolar nasal [n] where the older form of a word has none. English inserted an intrusive n before the /dʒ/ of several French-derived agent nouns in -ager: Middle English scavager and herbergeour became scavenger and harbinger, and Old French passagier gave passenger. Messenger has the same n, already present in its Middle English forms. Wiktionary gives contamination from suffixes such as Middle English -ing as an alternative explanation. Before /ɡ/ the inserted nasal is velar, as in nightingale (Middle English nightegale), which belongs to the ∅ > ŋ cell.

examples.from: Middle English scavager (< Anglo-Norman scawageour 'inspector, tax collector')
examples.note: Wiktionary compares messenger and passenger, which gained the same n before /dʒ/; passenger is from Old French passagier 'with intrusive n'.

examples.from: Middle English herberjour, herbergeour (< Old French herbergeor) 'one sent ahead to arrange lodgings'
